title: The Lantern-Keeper of the Fog
summary: On the fog-drowned moor, a keeper carries a lantern that guides lost travelers home — but each soul she saves costs her one of her own memories, and she has kept the light so long she has almost forgotten who she is. When Tam is sent to inherit the lantern, she must decide whether saving strangers is worth erasing yourself.

chapters.title: The Light on the Moor
chapters.body:
The moor above Greywither was drowned in fog more often than not, and in that fog, people got lost.

It was a particular kind of fog — thick, cold, and wrong, the sort that turned a ten-minute walk into a circling nightmare, that swallowed the path and the stars and the sound of your own village until you didn't know up from down or home from away. People walked into that fog and simply never came out. The moor had eaten travelers for as long as Greywither had stood beneath it.

Except that, sometimes, a lost traveler would see a light. A small warm lantern-glow, drifting in the grey, and they'd follow it, and it would lead them — gently, patiently, around the bogs and back to the path and down off the moor to safety. Everyone in Greywither had a grandparent or a cousin who'd been saved by the light in the fog. They called whoever carried it the Lantern-Keeper, and they left offerings of bread and wool at the foot of the moor, and they did not go up to look for her, because you did not seek the Lantern-Keeper. She found you, if you were lost, and if you were not lost you had no business on the moor.

Tam was fourteen, and she had been chosen.

She didn't know by whom, or how. She only knew that on her fourteenth birthday, the old headwoman of Greywither had come to her house with grey in her face and told Tam's parents that it was time, that the moor had named their daughter, that the Lantern-Keeper was fading and needed to pass the light on, and that Tam must go up into the fog and learn to carry it. Her parents wept, but they did not refuse. You did not refuse the moor. And so Tam climbed up into the grey, frightened and uncomprehending, to find the keeper of the light.

She found her in the heart of the fog, where the grey was thickest — a figure so faint she was almost fog herself, a thin old woman in a tattered cloak, holding a lantern that burned with a small warm unwavering flame. But when the old woman turned, Tam's breath caught. Because the keeper's face was strange and terrible: not old with wrinkles, but old with absence. Her eyes were kind and completely empty, like windows into a house where no one lived anymore. She looked at Tam the way you look at a stranger, and a beloved, and nothing at all, all at once.

"You've come," the keeper said, and her voice was soft and far away. "Good. I can't remember how long I've waited. I can't remember much of anything now. That's how I know it's time." She held out the lantern with a trembling hand. "Let me tell you what the light costs, child, while I still remember enough to tell you. Because they never tell you, down in the village. They just send you up. And you deserve to know what you're being asked to give."

chapters.title: What the Light Costs
chapters.body:
The old keeper sat Tam down on a cold stone in the heart of the fog, and told her the truth of the lantern.

"The light guides the lost home," she said. "That much is true, and it's a good and holy thing. Every soul that would have died on this moor, wandering in circles until the cold took them — the light saves them. Brings them back to the path, back to their families, back to their lives. I have saved more people than I can count." A ghost of a smile. "Truly. I cannot count them. Because that's the cost, child. Every soul the lantern guides home costs the keeper one of her own memories. The light doesn't burn oil. It burns the keeper's life — not her years, but her past. Every stranger I've led out of the fog, I paid for with a piece of myself."

Tam stared at her. "Your memories?"

"All of them, in the end." The keeper looked into the small warm flame. "I don't remember my name. I don't remember the village I came from, or my mother's face, or whether I had brothers, or what I loved, or who loved me. I don't remember being young. I don't remember choosing this, though I must have, once, the way you're being asked to choose now. Every time I lifted the lantern for a lost soul, the fog took something from me in exchange. And I lifted it so many times, for so many years, that there's almost nothing left. I'm not a person anymore, child. I'm just the light, and a hand to hold it, and a fading ghost of whoever I used to be." She turned her empty kind eyes on Tam. "That's what they're asking you to become. That's the price of saving the lost. You give yourself away, one memory at a time, until there's no self left — only the service."

Tam felt cold that had nothing to do with the fog. "Then why did you do it? Why would anyone?"

"Because people were dying," the keeper said simply. "And I could stop it. When you know you can save someone, and the only cost is yourself — it's a hard thing to say no to. It feels selfish to say no. How do you weigh your own memories against a stranger's whole life? So you lift the lantern. And then you lift it again. And each time it's just one more memory, one more soul, a fair trade, surely — and by the time you understand that you're disappearing, you've disappeared too far to stop." She pressed the lantern into Tam's hands. It was warm, and lighter than it looked, and Tam felt it immediately — a faint tugging at the edges of her mind, as if it were already reaching for something to burn. "Now it's yours. And I'm sorry. I'm so sorry, child. Someone has to carry it, or the moor goes back to eating everyone. But no one should have to carry it like I did. Alone. Emptying out. Forgetting even why."

And with those words, the last of the old keeper seemed to go out like a candle. Her faint form thinned into the fog, her empty kind eyes closing, and she was gone — not dead exactly, but finished, dissolved back into the grey she'd given herself to, having passed on the last thing she had.

Tam stood alone in the heart of the fog, holding a lantern that would save the lost by devouring her, one memory at a time, until she too was nothing but a light and a hand and a ghost.

And out in the grey, faint and frightened, she heard it: a voice. Someone lost. Someone calling. Someone wandering the cold moor in circles, about to die, unless she lifted the lantern and paid the price to bring them home.

chapters.title: The Keeper Who Refused to Vanish
chapters.body:
Tam almost lifted the lantern right then. The voice in the fog was so frightened, and so close to giving up, and she had the light, and she could save them — for the price of one memory she'd never miss.

But she had just watched what one memory at a time did to a person. She had looked into the empty kind eyes of a woman who'd given away everything — her name, her mother, her whole self — one fair trade at a time, until there was no one left to be grateful, no one left to have lived. And Tam understood, standing there with the warm devouring lantern in her hands, that the old keeper had been trapped not by the moor, but by a lie the moor told. The lie that it had to be all of you. The lie that saving others meant erasing yourself. The lie that there was no way to hold the light except to disappear behind it.

The old keeper had believed that lie because she'd carried the lantern alone, in the fog, with no one to tell her otherwise. She'd never questioned whether the terms could be different. She'd just paid, and paid, and paid, in secret, until she was gone.

But Tam was not going to pay in secret. And she was not going to pay alone.

First — because the voice was dying and this could not wait — she lifted the lantern. Just once. She let the light reach into her and take a memory: a small one, an ordinary morning, the taste of bread. She felt it go, felt the little emptiness where it had been, and she watched the warm glow drift out into the fog and find the lost traveler and lead them, gently, patiently, down off the moor to safety. One life saved. One piece of herself given. She understood, now, viscerally, how the old keeper had begun.

But then Tam did what the old keeper never had. She did not stay in the fog. She carried the lantern down off the moor, into Greywither, right into the square, and she stood before the whole village and told them the truth — the truth the headwoman had known and never spoken, the truth they'd all been content not to ask about while they left their bread and wool and let a woman disappear alone in the grey on their behalf.

"The light costs the keeper her memories," Tam told them, her voice shaking but clear. "Every soul it saves, it pays for with a piece of whoever holds it. The old keeper gave everything — her name, her whole life, all of it — alone, up there, while you left offerings and looked away. And you were about to let me do the same. Send one girl up into the fog to vanish, so the rest of you never have to." She held up the lantern. "Well, I won't vanish. But I won't stop saving people either. So we're going to do this differently."

And she told them how. The lantern took one memory per soul saved — so no one person would carry it long enough to be emptied. The village would share the keeping. Each person would take the lantern for a short while, save a few of the lost, give a few small memories they could spare, and then pass it on to the next, and the next, so that the weight was spread across a whole village instead of crushing one soul. A hundred people each giving a little would save just as many travelers as one person giving everything — but no one would disappear. No one would forget their mother's face. No one would dissolve into the fog.

It was not a simple thing to arrange. Some in Greywither didn't want to take their turn — it was easier, after all, to let one girl do it, to keep leaving bread at the foot of the moor and looking away. And Tam saw in their reluctance the same thing that had trapped the old keeper: the quiet willingness to let someone else vanish so you didn't have to give up anything yourself.

"That's the real fog," she told them. "Not the one on the moor. The one that lets us send someone else to disappear for us, and call it their duty, and feel fine about it. I'm not asking any of you to give everything. I'm asking all of you to give a little. That's the difference between a sacrifice and a slaughter — whether it's shared, or whether we just pick one person and use them up."

And one by one — slowly, reluctantly, then with something like relief — the people of Greywither agreed. They built a roster. They shared the light. And the lantern passed from hand to hand through the village, year after year, saving the lost from the moor as it always had — but now no keeper ever emptied out, because no keeper ever held it alone for long. Each gave a few small memories they could live without, and kept the rest — kept their names, their loves, their whole selves — and the moor was tamed not by one person's disappearance but by everyone's small shared sacrifice.

Tam carried the lantern often, more than most, because she'd been the first to understand. But she never let it take more than she could spare, and she never let anyone else take more than they could spare either, and she lived a long full life with her memories mostly intact — her mother's face, her childhood, her name, all of it kept.

And when she was very old, and it was her turn one last time, she carried the lantern up into the grey and thought of the empty-eyed keeper she'd met at fourteen, the woman who'd given everything alone and forgotten even why. "You don't have to disappear to save people," Tam said into the fog, to the ghost of her, wherever she'd gone. "You never did. It just felt that way, up here, alone. I'm sorry no one ever came to share it with you. But someone shared it after you. A whole village did. And the lost still come home — and now the keepers do too."

And she lifted the light one last time, gave one small memory to the grey, guided one more lost soul gently home, and then walked back down the moor to pass the lantern on — herself still whole, still Tam, still someone who had lived — to the next pair of waiting hands.
